report:
Based on available evidence, the answer leans toward "likely yes, but with important caveats" rather than a firm yes.

**What the evidence shows:**

A 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (published in *Frontiers in Psychiatry*) found that magnesium supplementation produced a statistically significant reduction in depression scores compared to control conditions (SMD: −0.919, 95% CI: −1.443 to −0.396) ([pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10783196](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10783196/)). This is a fairly large effect size, suggesting a real benefit — though the authors note the trials were small, varied in magnesium form/dose, and results were "controversial" prior to pooling.

A separate systematic review and meta-analysis in *BJPsych Open* looked at both dietary magnesium intake and mood, finding an inverse association between magnesium-rich diets and depression in cross-sectional studies (odds ratio ~0.66), though this association was weaker or absent in prospective (longitudinal) studies — suggesting dietary correlation doesn't necessarily prove causation ([cambridge.org/core/journals/bjpsych-open](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bjpsych-open/article/magnesium-and-mood-disorders-systematic-review-and-metaanalysis/9257DB9E4EAC7F0A5C5B84E63B4D3AEF)).

Mechanistically, magnesium's antidepressant potential is plausible: it modulates NMDA and GABA receptor activity in ways similar to some antidepressants, and low magnesium is linked to increased inflammation and stress reactivity, both implicated in depression ([mdpi.com/2072-6643/17/13/2216](https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/17/13/2216)).

**Conclusion:** Current trial-level evidence, especially pooled RCT data, supports magnesium supplementation modestly improving depressive symptoms, particularly in people with mild-to-moderate depression or magnesium insufficiency. However, studies remain limited in number and size, dosing/formulations vary, and effects in severe or clinically diagnosed major depressive disorder are less established. It's a reasonably promising adjunct, not a proven standalone treatment — so "yes" is a fair but qualified answer.
